questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how we see the Moon shine at night.
sequence: The Sun shines light on the Moon.
The light hits the Moon's surface.
The light bounces (reflects) off the Moon.
questions.explanation: The Moon has no light of its own. It reflects sunlight, and the reflected light travels to our eyes.

questions.stem: Match each space object to what it is.
pairs: a ball of hot glowing gas
a space rock that burns up in our air
questions.explanation: A star makes its own light. A planet orbits a star and a moon orbits a planet. A meteor is a "shooting star" and a satellite can send signals to us.

questions.stem: Put the first six planets in order, starting nearest the Sun.
questions.explanation: The order from the Sun is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. "My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming" helps you remember.

questions.stem: The Moon makes its own light.
questions.explanation: The Moon only looks bright because it reflects light from the Sun. The Sun is a star and makes its own light.

questions.stem: The Earth takes one ___ to go once around the ___.
questions.explanation: The Earth orbits the Sun once in a year. The Moon orbits the Earth.

questions.stem: What keeps the planets going around the Sun?
questions.explanation: The Sun's gravity pulls on the planets and keeps them in their paths (orbits).

questions.stem: Which of these are planets in our solar system? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Mars, Jupiter and Saturn are planets. The Sun is a star and the Moon is a moon that orbits the Earth.

questions.stem: Sort each object into star, planet or moon.
items: one of the four moons Galileo saw near Jupiter
questions.explanation: Stars make their own light. Planets travel around a star, and moons travel around a planet.

questions.stem: Match each scientist to what they discovered or said.
pairs: said the planets go around the Sun
wrote about how the universe began
questions.explanation: Aryabhata said the Earth spins, Copernicus put the Sun at the centre, Galileo used a telescope to find Jupiter's moons, and Dr Jamal Nazrul Islam of Chattogram studied the universe.

questions.stem: Why does the Moon shine at night if it has no light of its own?
questions.model_answer: Sunlight bounces off (reflects from) the Moon and reaches our eyes.
questions.explanation: We see the Moon because it reflects the Sun's light, just like a mirror reflects a torch beam.

questions.stem: Earth is the only planet we know that has living things.
questions.explanation: Earth has water, air and the right temperature for life. Scientists have not found living things on any other planet yet.

questions.stem: A meteor, or "shooting star", is really a…
options: star that has fallen to Earth
space rock burning up in our air
questions.explanation: A meteor is a small space rock that burns up as it hurtles through the air around Earth, making a bright streak. It is not a real star.

questions.stem: An artificial satellite is a machine that people send into space to orbit a planet.
questions.explanation: People build artificial satellites for TV, phones and weather. Bangabandhu Satellite-1 orbits the Earth and is Bangladesh's first.

questions.stem: Look at the planets in order from the Sun. Which number is the Earth?
questions.image_alt: The Sun and eight planets in a row, numbered 1 to 8 from the Sun (not to scale).
questions.explanation: Earth is the third planet from the Sun, after Mercury (1) and Venus (2). Mars is number 4.

questions.stem: Which number is Jupiter, the biggest planet?
questions.image_alt: The Sun and eight planets in a row, numbered 1 to 8 from the Sun (not to scale).
questions.explanation: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the biggest planet in the solar system. Saturn (6) comes next.

questions.stem: Match each number in the picture to its planet.
questions.image_alt: The Sun and eight planets in a row, numbered 1 to 8 from the Sun (not to scale).
questions.explanation: Counting out from the Sun: 1 Mercury, 2 Venus, 3 Earth, 4 Mars, 5 Jupiter, 6 Saturn, 7 Uranus, 8 Neptune.

questions.stem: In the picture, number 4 is Mars. Mars is nearer to the Sun than Earth is.
questions.image_alt: The Sun and eight planets in a row, numbered 1 to 8 from the Sun (not to scale).
questions.explanation: Earth is number 3 and Mars is number 4, so Mars is further from the Sun than Earth.

questions.stem: Match each picture to what it is.
questions.explanation: The Sun is a star. Saturn is a planet with rings. The Moon travels around the Earth, a meteor streaks across the sky, and a satellite is a machine that orbits.

questions.stem: Moung wants to see the Sun better, so he plans to look at it through dark sunglasses. What is the right advice?
options: It is safe for a minute.
questions.explanation: Never look at the Sun, even through sunglasses or a telescope. It can damage your eyes.

questions.stem: Nadia's family lives on an island where it is hard to lay cables. How can they get TV and internet?
options: by signals from the Moon's light
questions.explanation: A satellite such as Bangabandhu Satellite-1 sends TV and internet signals across Bangladesh, even to islands and hills.

questions.stem: A weather satellite sees a cyclone forming over the Bay of Bengal. How does this help people on the coast?
options: It warns them early so they can reach a shelter.
questions.explanation: Weather satellites help people see cyclones coming. An early warning gives families time to move to a cyclone shelter.

questions.stem: Raju makes a model of the solar system with eight balls of the same size. What can his model **not** show well?
options: that the Sun is in the middle
how big each planet really is
questions.explanation: His model shows the order and the number of planets, but the real planets are very different sizes (Jupiter is the biggest). Models also cannot show the huge distances.

questions.stem: In the simulation, what does the Moon do while the Earth moves?

sim.task: Open Gravity and Orbits. Choose Sun, Earth and Moon, then press play. Watch the Moon for a while. You can tick the box that shows the paths.

options: It stays still in the middle.
It travels around the Sun only.
questions.explanation: The Moon orbits the Earth. At the same time, the Earth and Moon travel together around the Sun.

questions.stem: In the simulation, the Earth goes once around the Sun in one year.

sim.task: Open Gravity and Orbits. Choose Sun and Earth, then press play. Watch the clock until the Earth has gone once around the Sun.

questions.explanation: The clock in the simulation shows that one orbit of the Earth around the Sun takes about one year.

questions.stem: In the simulation, you turn gravity off while the Earth is moving. What happens to the Earth?

sim.task: Open Gravity and Orbits. Choose Sun and Earth, then press play. While the Earth is going round, turn gravity off and watch what happens.

options: It keeps going round in a circle.
It moves off in a straight line.
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls the Earth towards the Sun and bends its path into an orbit. With no gravity, nothing pulls it, so it moves off in a straight line.

questions.stem: In 1610 Galileo saw four moons going around Jupiter. Why did this help Copernicus's idea?
options: It showed that Jupiter is the biggest planet.
It showed that not everything goes around the Earth.
It showed that the Moon makes its own light.
It showed that the Sun is a star.
questions.explanation: Copernicus said the planets go around the Sun. If four moons go around Jupiter, then Earth is not the centre of everything, which supported his idea.

questions.stem: Mina says, "The Sun is a planet because it is big and round." What is the best correction?
options: The Sun is a star that makes its own light.
The Sun is a moon because it is very hot.
The Sun is a planet because the Earth orbits it.
The Sun is a meteor because it is bright.
questions.explanation: A star is a ball of hot, glowing gas that makes its own light. The planets, including Earth, travel around our star, the Sun.

questions.stem: Why do you think there is life on Earth but not on Mercury?
questions.model_answer: Earth has water, air and the right temperature. Mercury is too hot by day, too cold by night, and has no air.
questions.explanation: Living things need water, air and a suitable temperature. Earth has all three. Mercury is very hot in the day, very cold at night, and has almost no air.
